title: Calculated pH from Specific Conductivity (Cycle Chemistry)
methodRef: Cycle chemistry practice for all-volatile treatment (AVT); basis EPRI/ASME feedwater guidelines
frequency: Every shift on feedwater and condensate; continuously where on-line instruments are fitted
holdingTime: ANALYSE ON-LINE OR IMMEDIATELY — high-purity samples absorb CO2 from air within seconds and the reading is then meaningless
equipment: On-line or bench specific conductivity meter with automatic temperature compensation to 25 °C
Sample cooler and flow-through cell (a flowing sample is essential)
Low-ionic-strength pH electrode with flow cell (for comparison only)
reagents: Cation exchange resin (hydrogen form) for the cation column
interferences: Atmospheric CO2 is the dominant error source — a grab sample exposed to air gains conductivity and loses pH within seconds. Always sample from a flowing, closed line.
Any contamination (condenser leak, carryover, resin fines) invalidates the calculation entirely, because the method assumes the alkalising agent is the ONLY significant ionic species.
If an amine other than ammonia is dosed (morpholine, cyclohexylamine, ETA), the cation conductivity constant differs and the ammonia-based result will be wrong.
A conductivity reading not compensated to 25 °C will give a badly wrong pH — confirm the meter's compensation is active and set correctly.
steps: CONFIRM THE METHOD APPLIES: this calculation is valid only for high-purity cycle water (feedwater, condensate, makeup) dosed with ammonia or an amine. It is NOT valid for boiler drum water with solid alkali (phosphate/caustic), cooling water, or raw water.

Establish a continuous flow through the sample cooler and conditioning system. Let the sample flow long enough to fully purge the line — a stagnant line reads the previous condition, not the current one.
Verify the sample temperature at the analyser is within the meter's range and that automatic temperature compensation to 25 °C is enabled.
Read and record the SPECIFIC conductivity (µS/cm at 25 °C) from the flowing sample.
Read and record the CATION (acid) conductivity from the same sample point. This is the critical validity check: it strips the ammonia and leaves only contaminant anions.

ASSESS VALIDITY BEFORE CALCULATING: cation conductivity should be very low relative to specific conductivity (typically well under 0.2 µS/cm on a clean cycle). If cation conductivity is elevated or climbing, the sample is contaminated — investigate the source and do NOT report a calculated pH as if it were valid.
Enter the specific conductivity into the pH from Specific Conductivity calculator, along with the cation conductivity for the contamination ratio check.
If an amine other than ammonia is in use, change the cation equivalent conductivity input to the value supplied by your chemical vendor for that amine. The 73.5 default is ammonia.

Compare the calculated pH to the on-line pH instrument reading. In clean high-purity water the calculated value is generally the MORE reliable of the two, because glass pH electrodes respond poorly in low-conductivity water.

If calculated and measured pH disagree by more than the site's tolerance: suspect the pH electrode first (calibration, ageing, low-ionic-strength error, grounding), then suspect contamination — check whether cation conductivity moved at the same time.

Use the Expected Conductivity from Target pH calculator in reverse to set or verify the control band: it gives the specific conductivity that should correspond to your target cycle pH, plus the ammonia concentration needed to hold it.

Log specific conductivity, cation conductivity, calculated pH, measured pH, and ammonia feed rate together in the Logbook. Trending all of them side by side is what identifies a developing condenser leak early.
qualityControl: Verify the conductivity meter against a low-range standard on the schedule set by your QA programme; low-range cells drift and foul.
Regenerate or replace the cation column resin per schedule — an exhausted column silently reports falsely low cation conductivity, hiding contamination.
Cross-check calculated pH against measured pH every shift and record both; a widening gap is itself a diagnostic.
Confirm the calculation is being used only within its valid range (clean, ammoniated high-purity water).
troubleshooting: Calculated pH much higher than measured pH: usually a tired or poorly grounded pH electrode in low-conductivity water — verify the electrode before changing chemical feed.
Specific conductivity rising while cation conductivity stays flat: more ammonia is being dosed — a feed rate change, not contamination.

BOTH specific and cation conductivity rising: contamination ingress (condenser leak, air in-leakage producing CO2, makeup breakthrough). Treat as a chemistry excursion and follow the site's action-level response.
Conductivity below the pure-water minimum of about 0.055 µS/cm: the reading or its temperature compensation is faulty — no real sample can read below this.
safetyNotes: Sample lines carry high-temperature, high-pressure water — confirm the sample cooler is in service and the sample is at a safe temperature before opening any valve.
Never open a sample line whose cooling water flow is not confirmed.
Ammonia solutions release irritating vapour — handle feed chemicals in a ventilated area with eye protection.

title: Cooling Tower Cycles of Concentration — Monitoring
frequency: Daily on cooling towers; more often during high-load or high-evaporation periods
holdingTime: Analyse promptly; conductivity and chloride are stable but biological activity can alter samples on standing
equipment: Chloride test kit or Hach digital titrator (alternative tracer)
Clean sample bottles, clearly labelled for makeup and blowdown
reagents: Chloride titration reagents (silver nitrate / mercuric nitrate kit) if using the chloride method
interferences: The two samples MUST be taken at the same time — makeup quality varies through the day and comparing samples taken hours apart gives a meaningless ratio.

Any tracer that is added, consumed, or lost in the system is invalid. Conductivity is affected by treatment chemical dosing; chloride is usually the more reliable tracer where chemicals are dosed heavily.
Recent make-up surges, blowdown events, or heavy rain (on open towers) temporarily distort the ratio.
steps: Collect a makeup water sample and a tower basin/blowdown sample at the SAME time, from established sample points.
Label both bottles immediately — mixing them up inverts the result.
Let both samples reach the same temperature before measuring, or rely on the meter's temperature compensation.
Calibrate/verify the conductivity meter against a standard.
Rinse the probe with deionised water then with sample, and measure the conductivity of the MAKEUP sample. Record it.
Rinse again and measure the conductivity of the BLOWDOWN/basin sample. Record it.
If using chloride as the tracer instead, titrate both samples per the chloride kit instructions and record both values in mg/L Cl.
Enter both values into the Cycles of Concentration calculator. Both inputs must be the same parameter and the same units.
Compare the result to the target COC for the system. Running below target wastes water and chemical; running above target risks scaling and fouling.
If the COC is off target, use the Cooling Tower Blowdown Rate calculator with the current evaporation rate to determine the blowdown rate needed to bring it back.
Before changing blowdown, check the corrosion inhibitor and biocide residuals — changing blowdown changes their concentration too.
Log makeup value, blowdown value, calculated COC, target COC, and any blowdown adjustment made in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Verify the conductivity meter daily against a standard.
Cross-check the conductivity-based COC against a chloride-based COC periodically; a large disagreement means one tracer is being affected by treatment chemistry.
Track COC daily — a sudden change usually means a blowdown valve issue or a makeup water change, not a real chemistry shift.
Confirm sample points are the correct, established ones each time.
troubleshooting: COC calculates as less than 1: the samples were swapped, or the makeup reading is contaminated. Repeat with fresh samples.
COC much higher than expected: blowdown valve may be closed, blocked, or failed shut — verify physically.
COC much lower than expected: blowdown stuck open, or excessive drift/leakage losses.
COC swings day to day with no operational change: check whether the makeup sample point is picking up recirculated water.
safetyNotes: Cooling tower water may contain Legionella — avoid creating aerosols, wear appropriate PPE, and follow the site's cooling water sampling precautions.
Wash hands thoroughly after handling cooling water samples.

title: Boiler Blowdown — Procedure and Sampling
methodRef: Standard boiler water sampling practice (ASME guidance basis)
frequency: Per shift on operating boilers; after any load change or chemistry excursion
holdingTime: Analyse promptly after cooling; keep the sample capped to limit CO2 pick-up
equipment: Sample cooler with confirmed cooling water flow
Conductivity meter, pH meter, and any reagent test kits required by the treatment programme
interferences: An inadequately flushed sample line gives the previous sample's chemistry, not the current boiler condition.
A hot sample gives wrong conductivity and pH readings and is a burn hazard — always cool to a controlled temperature first.
Samples left open absorb CO2, lowering pH and raising conductivity.
steps: BEFORE OPENING ANY VALVE: confirm the sample cooler is in service and cooling water is flowing. Verify by touch on the cooling water outlet, not by assumption.
Put on heat-resistant gloves and a face shield. Boiler water is at drum pressure and temperature.
Crack the sample valve open slowly. Never open a boiler sample valve quickly — flashing steam causes severe burns.

Flush the sample line for at least 1-2 minutes, and long enough for the sample temperature to stabilise at the cooler outlet. Confirm the sample is at a safe handling temperature (typically below 40 °C) before collecting.
Rinse the sample bottle with the flowing sample, then fill it, capping immediately to limit CO2 absorption.
Close the sample valve fully and confirm it is not passing.
Measure pH and conductivity promptly on the cooled sample, plus any programme-specific parameters (phosphate, sulfite, silica, alkalinity).
Enter the feedwater TDS and the maximum allowed boiler water TDS into the Boiler % Blowdown calculator to determine the blowdown percentage required.
Compare the measured boiler water TDS/conductivity to the site limit for the operating pressure. Exceeding the limit risks carryover, foaming, and turbine or superheater deposits.
Adjust continuous blowdown as required, in small increments, and re-sample after the system has had time to respond — do not chase the reading with large rapid changes.
Verify intermittent (bottom) blowdown is being carried out per schedule; it removes settled sludge that continuous blowdown does not.
Log the sample time, boiler ID, all measured parameters, blowdown setting before and after, and any adjustment made in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Confirm meters are calibrated before the shift's first sample.
Trend boiler water conductivity against feedwater conductivity — the ratio should be consistent with the blowdown rate in service.
Repeat any result that exceeds a control limit on a fresh sample before taking corrective action.
Record the sample cooler outlet temperature; a rising trend means the cooler is fouling.
troubleshooting: Boiler TDS climbing despite blowdown at setpoint: blowdown valve passing insufficient flow, blocked line, or increased feedwater solids — check feedwater quality and the valve.
Boiler TDS falling rapidly with no setting change: blowdown valve failed open, or a sudden rise in condensate return fraction.
Sample too hot at the cooler outlet: cooling water flow inadequate or cooler fouled. STOP and correct before continuing.
pH drifting down across the shift with stable conductivity: possible CO2 absorption in sampling, or loss of alkalinity control.
safetyNotes: SCALDING HAZARD: boiler water is above 100 °C at pressure and flashes to steam on release. Never sample without a functioning sample cooler.
Open sample valves slowly and stand to the side of the discharge.
Boiler water is highly alkaline and causes severe eye and skin burns — full PPE including face shield is required.
Never leave a boiler sample valve unattended while open.

title: Silica — Hach Silicomolybdate (DR6000)
methodRef: Hach Method 8185 — Silicomolybdate; equivalent to SM 4500-SiO2 C
hachMethod: Method 8185 — Silicomolybdate (high range). Method 8186 (Heteropoly Blue) for low range.
range: 1 – 100 mg/L SiO2 (silicomolybdate); use the low-range heteropoly blue method below 1 mg/L
wavelength: 452 nm (set automatically by the stored program)
frequency: Daily on boiler water and feedwater; every shift on high-pressure units
holdingTime: Analyse within 24 h. NEVER store samples in glass — glass leaches silica and biases results high. Use plastic bottles only.
reagents: Deionised, silica-free water for the blank
interferences: PHOSPHATE is the major interference — the citric acid step exists specifically to destroy the phosphomolybdate complex and MUST NOT be skipped or shortened. Boiler water on a phosphate programme always contains phosphate.
Glass containers and glass pipettes leach silica into the sample. Use plastic throughout wherever possible.
Sulfide and high colour interfere.
Reaction timing is critical — this method depends on a timed sequence, not just a final reading.
steps: Collect the sample in a clean PLASTIC bottle. Cool boiler water samples through the sample cooler first and let them reach room temperature.

Power on the DR6000 and select the stored program for silica by the silicomolybdate method (Hach Method 8185). Confirm the program on the instrument — program numbers vary by firmware; the method number is the stable reference.
Fill a clean sample cell to the 10 mL mark with sample.
Add the molybdate 3 reagent as specified in the Hach procedure and swirl to mix.
Start the instrument timer for the molybdate reaction period and let it run to completion. During this period the silicomolybdate (and any phosphomolybdate) complex forms.
Add the citric acid reagent, swirl to dissolve, and start the second timed period. This step destroys the phosphate interference — do not read before this timer completes.
PREPARE THE BLANK using the untreated sample in a second matched cell (per the Hach procedure for this method).
Wipe both cells thoroughly with a lint-free wipe before every insertion.
Insert the blank, close the lid, and press ZERO.
Insert the prepared sample in the same orientation, close the lid, and press READ. Record the result in mg/L SiO2.
If the result is above the method range, dilute with silica-free deionised water using plastic labware, re-run, and multiply by the dilution factor.
Enter the boiler water silica result and the maximum allowed silica for your operating pressure (from the ASME/manufacturer chart) into the Silica Carryover Check calculator.
Interpret against operating pressure: allowable silica falls sharply as drum pressure rises, because volatile silica carryover into steam causes hard, non-removable turbine blade deposits.
If silica is approaching the limit, increase blowdown and investigate the source — usually makeup water breakthrough from an exhausted demineraliser or softener.
Log the silica result, the drum pressure, the limit applied, and any blowdown change in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Run a silica-free deionised water blank with each batch — a positive blank usually means glass contamination somewhere in the process.
Verify against a known silica standard on the QA schedule.
Run a duplicate on every 10th sample.
Record reagent lot numbers and expiry dates; silica reagents degrade and give low results when old.
troubleshooting: Results consistently biased high: silica contamination from glassware — switch entirely to plastic and re-run.
Results biased high on a phosphate-treated boiler: the citric acid step was skipped or under-timed. Repeat with full timing.
Result unexpectedly low on a known-high sample: check for over-range (dilute and repeat) and confirm reagent is in date.
Poor reproducibility: timing is being applied inconsistently — use the instrument timer for every step, every time.
safetyNotes: Acid and molybdate reagents are corrosive and irritant — wear gloves and eye protection.
Cool boiler water samples fully before handling; see the boiler sampling procedure for scalding precautions.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Phosphate, Reactive — Hach PhosVer 3 (DR6000)
methodRef: Hach Method 8048 — PhosVer 3 (ascorbic acid); equivalent to SM 4500-P E
hachMethod: Method 8048 — PhosVer 3 powder pillows (ascorbic acid method)
range: 0.02 – 2.50 mg/L PO4 (dilute boiler water samples, which are normally well above this)
wavelength: 880 nm (set automatically by the stored program)
frequency: Per shift on boilers under a phosphate treatment programme
holdingTime: Analyse within 48 h; store at 4 °C. Do not use containers washed with phosphate-containing detergent.
equipment: Volumetric flasks and pipettes for dilution (boiler water almost always needs diluting)
reagents: Deionised water for dilution and blank
interferences: PHOSPHATE-CONTAINING DETERGENTS are a serious contamination source — never wash silica or phosphate glassware with them. Rinse thoroughly with deionised water.
High turbidity or colour in the sample biases results; filter if necessary.
Large amounts of iron or silica interfere at their upper limits.
The blue colour continues to develop with time — read within the window specified by the method for consistent results.
steps: Collect a boiler water sample through the sample cooler and allow it to cool to room temperature.

DILUTE FIRST: boiler water phosphate residuals are typically maintained well above the 2.50 mg/L method range. Prepare an accurate dilution with deionised water (e.g. 1:10 or 1:20) using volumetric glassware, and record the exact dilution factor.
Select the stored program for reactive phosphorus by PhosVer 3 (Hach Method 8048) on the DR6000. Confirm the program on the instrument.
PREPARE THE BLANK: fill a clean cell to the 10 mL mark with the diluted, unreacted sample.
Wipe the blank cell with a lint-free wipe, insert it, close the lid, and press ZERO.
PREPARE THE SAMPLE: fill the second matched cell to the 10 mL mark with the diluted sample.
Add the contents of one PhosVer 3 powder pillow, cap, and shake to dissolve.
Start the 2-minute instrument timer. A blue colour develops if phosphate is present.
When the timer expires, wipe the cell, insert it in the same orientation as the blank, and press READ.
Multiply the displayed result by the dilution factor to get the true boiler water phosphate concentration. Record both the raw reading and the corrected result so the dilution is auditable.
Compare to the target residual band for your treatment programme and drum pressure.
If the residual is off target, use the Phosphate Residual Dosing calculator with the feed/blowdown flow to determine the chemical feed adjustment in kg/day.
Consider the pH and phosphate together — congruent/coordinated phosphate programmes control both, and phosphate alone does not tell the full story.
Log the raw reading, dilution factor, corrected result, target band, and any dosing change in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Run a deionised water blank with reagent to confirm no phosphate contamination in glassware or water.
Verify against a prepared phosphate standard on the QA schedule.
Run a duplicate on every 10th sample; include the dilution step in the duplicate so dilution error is captured.
Record reagent lot and expiry.
troubleshooting: Result at the very top of the range: dilution was insufficient — dilute further and repeat rather than reporting a near-range value.
Persistently high blank: glassware contaminated by phosphate detergent — re-wash and rinse thoroughly with deionised water.
Blue colour weak or absent on a sample known to contain phosphate: reagent expired, or the sample was over-diluted.
Poor duplicate agreement: the dilution step is the usual culprit — use volumetric glassware, not graduated cylinders.
safetyNotes: PhosVer 3 reagent contains an acid salt — avoid skin and eye contact.
Cool boiler water samples fully before handling.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Hydrazine — Hach p-Dimethylaminobenzaldehyde (DR6000)
range: Low µg/L to low mg/L N2H4 — confirm the exact range for your reagent set on the instrument
frequency: Per shift on feedwater where hydrazine is the oxygen scavenger
holdingTime: ANALYSE IMMEDIATELY — hydrazine oxidises rapidly on exposure to air and the result falls within minutes
reagents: Hydrazine reagent (PDAB) per the Hach method
interferences: Air exposure destroys hydrazine — sample from a flowing line into a filled, capped container with no headspace.
Other reducing agents and some amines can interfere.
Temperature affects colour development; blank and sample must match.
steps: Sample from a flowing, cooled sample line. Fill the container completely with no air space and cap immediately.
Take the sample to the instrument and analyse without delay — hydrazine results are only meaningful when the test is run immediately.
Select the stored program for hydrazine (Hach Method 8141) on the DR6000 and confirm it matches your reagent set.
Prepare the blank and sample exactly per the Hach method sheet for this method, using the instrument's built-in timer for the colour development period.
Wipe both cells with a lint-free wipe before insertion.
Zero on the blank, then read the sample and record the result.

Compare to the target residual for your treatment programme. Too little hydrazine leaves dissolved oxygen free to cause pitting corrosion; excessive hydrazine wastes chemical and can contribute to ammonia formation in the cycle.
Cross-check against the dissolved oxygen reading from the same part of the cycle — the two should tell a consistent story.
Log the hydrazine residual, the dissolved oxygen result, the feed rate, and the sample point in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Run a deionised water blank with reagent.
Verify against a freshly prepared hydrazine standard on the QA schedule — hydrazine standards degrade, so prepare them fresh.
Duplicate results should be taken back-to-back, since the analyte itself decays with time.
troubleshooting: Result reads near zero on a dosed system: almost always air exposure during sampling. Re-sample with no headspace and analyse immediately.
Results consistently drifting down through the shift: check the scavenger feed pump and the storage tank level.
Poor reproducibility: timing or air exposure. Use the instrument timer and minimise handling.
safetyNotes: HYDRAZINE IS TOXIC AND A SUSPECTED CARCINOGEN. Handle with gloves and eye protection in a well-ventilated area; avoid inhaling vapour and avoid all skin contact.
Follow your site's specific controls for hydrazine handling and disposal — do not pour to drain without checking the site procedure.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Iron, Total — Hach FerroVer (DR6000)
hachMethod: Method 8008 — FerroVer iron reagent powder pillows
wavelength: 510 nm (set automatically by the stored program)
frequency: Weekly on feedwater and condensate; daily during commissioning, after chemical cleaning, or during a corrosion investigation
holdingTime: Analyse promptly. For total iron, acidify to pH < 2 with nitric acid if storage is required — iron adsorbs onto container walls otherwise.
reagents: FerroVer Iron Reagent powder pillows, 10 mL
Nitric acid for sample preservation (if storing)
interferences: Iron plates out onto container walls quickly — analyse fresh or acidify immediately.
Insoluble iron oxide particles (the main corrosion product of interest) may not fully dissolve without a digestion step; FerroVer dissolves most but not all forms.
High turbidity biases the result high — the blank correction handles sample colour but not particulates.
Strong oxidisers and high concentrations of copper interfere.
steps: Collect the sample from a flowing, cooled sample line into an acid-washed plastic bottle. Corrosion product iron is often particulate, so collect a well-mixed representative sample.
Select the stored program for total iron by FerroVer (Hach Method 8008) on the DR6000 and confirm it on the instrument.
Fill a clean sample cell to the 10 mL mark with sample; this is the blank.
Fill the second matched cell to the 10 mL mark with sample and add the contents of one FerroVer powder pillow. Swirl to dissolve.
Start the 3-minute instrument timer. An orange colour develops if iron is present.
Wipe the blank cell, insert it, close the lid, and press ZERO.
When the timer expires, wipe the prepared cell, insert it in the same orientation, and press READ. Record the result in mg/L Fe.

Interpret in context: iron in feedwater and condensate is a direct measure of corrosion happening in the cycle. A rising trend indicates active corrosion even when pH and oxygen scavenger residuals look acceptable.
If iron is elevated, review feedwater pH (calculated pH from conductivity), oxygen scavenger residual, and dissolved oxygen together — iron is the outcome, those are the causes.
Log the result with the sample point and the corresponding pH/oxygen data in the Logbook, and trend it over weeks rather than judging a single reading.
qualityControl: Run a deionised water blank with reagent.
Verify against an iron standard on the QA schedule.
Run duplicates on every 10th sample; particulate iron makes duplicates less repeatable than dissolved analytes, so poor agreement may be real sample heterogeneity.
Use acid-washed bottles dedicated to iron sampling.
troubleshooting: Results scatter widely between duplicates: particulate iron is unevenly distributed — mix thoroughly and consider a digestion step for total iron.
Low results on a system with visible red/black deposits: iron is present as insoluble oxide that FerroVer alone is not dissolving; a digestion procedure is required.
High blank: contaminated cells or bottles — acid wash and rinse with deionised water.
safetyNotes: FerroVer reagent is an irritant — avoid skin and eye contact.
Nitric acid used for preservation is highly corrosive and oxidising — handle in a fume hood with full PPE.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Copper — Hach Bicinchoninate (DR6000)
wavelength: 560 nm (set automatically by the stored program)
frequency: Weekly on condensate and feedwater where copper alloys are present in the cycle
holdingTime: Analyse promptly; acidify to pH < 2 for storage
reagents: CuVer / bicinchoninate copper reagent powder pillows
interferences: Copper adsorbs to container walls — use acid-washed bottles and analyse promptly.
High iron concentrations can interfere.
Sample turbidity biases results; the blank correction handles colour but not particulates.
steps: Collect the sample from a flowing, cooled sample line into an acid-washed bottle.
Select the stored program for copper by the bicinchoninate method (Hach Method 8506) on the DR6000.
Fill a clean cell to the 10 mL mark with sample for the blank; wipe and zero the instrument on it.
Fill the second matched cell to the 10 mL mark, add one copper reagent powder pillow, and swirl to dissolve.
Run the instrument's timed reaction period. A purple colour develops if copper is present.
Wipe the cell, insert in the same orientation, and press READ. Record in mg/L Cu.

Interpret in context: copper in the cycle indicates corrosion of copper-alloy condenser tubes or feedwater heaters. Copper deposits on turbine blades and boiler tubes are particularly damaging and difficult to remove.

Review feedwater pH and ammonia together with copper — excessive ammonia in the presence of oxygen attacks copper alloys, so a high copper trend may mean the pH/ammonia setpoint needs review for a mixed-metallurgy cycle.
Log the result with the sample point, feedwater pH, and ammonia level in the Logbook and trend over time.
qualityControl: Run a deionised water blank with reagent.
Verify against a copper standard on the QA schedule.
Run duplicates on every 10th sample.
Dedicate acid-washed glassware to trace metals work.
troubleshooting: Low or zero result despite known copper corrosion: copper may be present as particulate oxide requiring digestion.
High blank: container or cell contamination — acid wash thoroughly.
Erratic results: adsorption losses; analyse fresh samples and acidify anything held.
safetyNotes: Reagent is an irritant — avoid skin and eye contact.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Molybdate (Corrosion Inhibitor) — Hach (DR6000)
methodRef: Hach Method 8036 — Mercaptoacetic acid method for molybdenum/molybdate
range: 0.3 – 40.0 mg/L Mo (confirm the range for your reagent set)
frequency: Daily to weekly on cooling systems dosed with a molybdate-based inhibitor, per the treatment programme
reagents: Molybdenum reagent set per Hach Method 8036
interferences: Cooling water is often turbid and biologically active — filter the sample if turbidity is significant.
High concentrations of other treatment chemicals can interfere.
Sample and blank must be at the same temperature.
steps: Collect a representative cooling system sample from an established, flowing sample point.
Filter the sample if it is visibly turbid, since suspended solids bias colorimetric readings.
Select the stored program for molybdenum (Hach Method 8036) on the DR6000.
Prepare the blank and sample per the Hach method sheet for your reagent set, using the instrument timer for each timed step.
Wipe both cells, zero on the blank, then read the sample and record the result.
Compare the inhibitor residual to the target band set by your chemical vendor. Under-dosing leaves metal unprotected; over-dosing wastes chemical and may create discharge compliance issues.
Consider the residual alongside the cycles of concentration — as COC changes, inhibitor concentration changes with it, so a residual drift may reflect a blowdown change rather than a feed problem.
Log the residual, the COC, the inhibitor feed rate, and any adjustment in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Run a blank with each batch.
Verify against a standard on the QA schedule.
Run duplicates on every 10th sample.
Cross-check the residual trend against the chemical consumption from the day tank — a residual that falls while consumption stays flat suggests a system loss.
troubleshooting: Residual falls with no feed change: increased blowdown, a system leak, or inhibitor consumption by fresh metal surfaces.
Residual climbs steadily: blowdown reduced or failed closed — verify COC.
Erratic results: sample turbidity — filter before analysis.
safetyNotes: Molybdate reagents are irritants — avoid skin and eye contact.
Cooling water may contain Legionella — avoid aerosols and follow site precautions.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Sulfite Residual — Titration Method
methodRef: Standard Methods 4500-SO3 / Hach digital titrator Method 8071
frequency: Per shift on boilers using sulfite as the oxygen scavenger
holdingTime: ANALYSE IMMEDIATELY — sulfite oxidises within minutes of air exposure
equipment: Sample cooler with a delivery tube long enough to reach the bottom of the flask
reagents: Standard titrant per the kit (e.g. potassium iodate-iodide)
interferences: AIR EXPOSURE is the dominant error — every second of contact with air lowers the result. This is the single biggest cause of falsely low sulfite readings.
Other reducing agents in the boiler water can titrate along with sulfite.
A hot sample loses sulfite faster; cool the sample before collection.
steps: Cool the sample through the sample cooler to below about 40 °C before collecting.
Collect the sample with the delivery tube reaching the BOTTOM of the flask, and let the flask overflow several volumes. This displaces air rather than mixing it in.
Cap or cover the sample and take it straight to the bench — analyse within seconds to minutes, not later.
Measure the sample volume specified by your kit into the titration flask, again minimising splashing and agitation.
Acidify the sample as directed by the method.
Add starch indicator.
Titrate with the standard titrant, swirling gently, to the first permanent blue-black colour that persists for about 30 seconds.
Record the titrant volume and convert to mg/L sulfite per your kit's conversion factor.
Compare to the target residual band for your programme and boiler pressure.
If the residual is off target, use the Sulfite Residual Dosing calculator with feedwater flow to determine the feed adjustment in kg/day.
Log the residual, the feedwater dissolved oxygen if available, and any feed change in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Run duplicates back-to-back, since the analyte decays with time.
Verify the titrant against a standard on the QA schedule.
If a result is unexpectedly low, ALWAYS repeat with careful air-free sampling before adjusting chemical feed — a sampling artefact and a genuine loss of residual look identical on the bench sheet.
troubleshooting: Consistently low or zero residual: air exposure during sampling is far more likely than genuine total depletion. Re-sample with the tube at the flask bottom and overflow generously.
Endpoint colour fades quickly: titrate slightly further and confirm the colour holds for 30 seconds.
Residual high but dissolved oxygen also high: the scavenger may not be reacting — check feed point location and water temperature at the point of injection.
safetyNotes: Cool samples fully — see the boiler sampling procedure for scalding precautions.
Sulfuric acid is corrosive; wear gloves and eye protection.
Boiler water is highly alkaline and causes burns.

title: Feedwater and Condensate Sampling
frequency: Per shift on all monitored cycle sample points
holdingTime: Analyse immediately — high-purity samples change rapidly on exposure to air
equipment: Sample coolers with confirmed cooling water flow
Clean, dedicated sample bottles (plastic for silica, acid-washed for metals)
Conductivity, cation conductivity, and pH instruments
interferences: CO2 and oxygen pick-up from air changes conductivity, pH, and dissolved oxygen within seconds — high-purity sampling must be done from a continuously flowing line.
Insufficient line flushing gives the previous condition rather than the current one.
Shared or improperly cleaned bottles cross-contaminate trace analyses.
steps: Confirm cooling water is flowing to every sample cooler being used before opening any sample valve.
Establish a continuous flow at the sample panel and let each line flush thoroughly — high-purity lines need generous flushing to reach true composition.
Verify the sample temperature at the panel is stable and safe to handle.
Take on-line readings first where fitted: specific conductivity, cation conductivity, pH, and dissolved oxygen. These are the most reliable because the sample never contacts air.
For any grab sample, fill the bottle completely with no headspace, overflowing several volumes, and cap immediately.
Use the correct bottle for each analysis: plastic for silica, acid-washed for iron and copper, and dedicated bottles for trace work.
Run time-sensitive tests first — dissolved oxygen, hydrazine, and sulfite degrade fastest.
Calculate the feedwater pH from specific conductivity using the calculated pH tool, and compare it to the measured pH.

Record the condensate and feedwater flows and use the Condensate Return % calculator to track the return fraction. A falling return percentage means more raw makeup entering the cycle, which brings more contamination and more chemical demand.

Cross-check the whole picture before concluding: conductivity, cation conductivity, pH, oxygen, iron, and copper together tell a consistent story; any single reading out of line with the rest is usually an instrument or sampling problem.
Log every parameter, the sample point, and the time in the Logbook. Consistent sample timing is what makes the trend usable.
qualityControl: Verify all meters against standards at the start of the shift.
Confirm sample line flows are within the panel's design range — too low a flow gives unrepresentative samples.
Track cation conductivity as the primary contamination indicator on every sample.
Repeat any out-of-limit result on a fresh sample before declaring a chemistry excursion.
troubleshooting: All parameters drift together across the shift: suspect the sample panel (flow, cooler fouling) before suspecting the plant.
Dissolved oxygen high on a deaerated system: usually air in-leakage at the sampling system rather than in the cycle — check sample line fittings first.
Conductivity higher on grab samples than on-line: CO2 absorption during sampling. Trust the on-line reading.
Condensate return percentage dropping: check for a condensate dump to drain, or a steam trap/leak losing condensate.
safetyNotes: SCALDING HAZARD — never open a sample valve without confirmed cooling water flow.
Open valves slowly and stand clear of the discharge path.
Cycle samples may contain hydrazine or ammonia — follow the relevant chemical handling precautions.

title: Conductivity Measurement
frequency: Per shift on all monitored points; continuous on-line where fitted
holdingTime: Measure on-line or immediately; high-purity samples change within seconds of air exposure
equipment: Conductivity meter with automatic temperature compensation
Conductivity cell matched to the range being measured (low-range cell for high-purity water)
reagents: Conductivity calibration standards appropriate to the range (e.g. 1413 µS/cm for general use, low-range standards for high-purity work)
interferences: Temperature has a large effect (roughly 2 % per °C) — automatic temperature compensation to 25 °C is essential, and its reference must be set correctly.
High-purity water absorbs CO2 from air almost instantly, raising conductivity. Static grab samples of condensate or demineralised water cannot be measured accurately.
A fouled or damaged cell reads low and responds slowly.
Using a general-purpose cell on high-purity water gives poor resolution at the low end.
steps: Select a cell with a cell constant appropriate to the expected range — do not use a high-range cell for high-purity water.
Calibrate or verify against a standard solution close to the expected sample conductivity. Record the result.
Confirm automatic temperature compensation is enabled and referenced to 25 °C.
For high-purity samples, use a flow-through cell on a continuously flowing line. Do not attempt a static beaker measurement.
For general samples, rinse the probe with deionised water, then with sample, and immerse fully with no bubbles trapped in the cell.
Allow the reading to stabilise completely before recording.
Record specific conductivity in µS/cm together with the sample temperature.

CATION (ACID) CONDUCTIVITY: pass the sample through the hydrogen-form cation exchange column and measure the effluent conductivity. This removes the alkalising agent and leaves contaminant anions, making it the sensitive indicator of ingress.
Use the Boiler Water TDS from Conductivity calculator where an estimated TDS is required, and the pH from Specific Conductivity calculator for high-purity cycle water.
Log specific conductivity, cation conductivity, and temperature for each point in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Verify calibration daily against a standard in the relevant range.
Track the cell constant over time; a drifting constant means the cell needs cleaning or replacement.
Replace or regenerate cation column resin on schedule — an exhausted column hides contamination by reading falsely low.
Compare on-line and bench readings periodically to confirm both are trustworthy.
troubleshooting: Reading low and slow to respond: fouled cell or trapped bubbles — clean the cell and re-immerse.
High-purity reading much higher than expected: CO2 absorption from a static or poorly flushed sample. Use a flowing sample.
Reading below 0.055 µS/cm: physically impossible for water at 25 °C — the meter or its compensation is faulty.
On-line and bench readings disagree: check both calibrations and confirm the bench sample was taken from a flowing line.
safetyNotes: Confirm sample coolers are in service before drawing hot samples.
Calibration standards should be poured into a beaker for use and never returned to the stock bottle.
